opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think people sometimes see it as a detour from AGI when it's really one of the most direct paths toward it.

Coding is a domain where you can see very clearly whether the model is actually reasoning. Code either runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. That gives you an incredibly rich, verifiable signal, which is exactly what you want when you're trying to push models to think harder, plan over longer horizons, and recover from their own mistakes. A lot of the capabilities we care about for general intelligence, like breaking a big problem into pieces, holding a lot of context in your head, and iterating until something works, show up in their purest form in software engineering.

There's also a leverage argument. Software is how so much of the world gets built now. If you can give every person the ability to turn an idea into working software, or give an engineer a team of agents that can take on whole tasks while they focus on the hard design decisions, you're amplifying human capability across almost every field. That's very close to the heart of what we mean when we say we want AGI to benefit everyone.

And then there's the flywheel. Better coding models help us build better tools, better infrastructure, and eventually help with the research itself. So the focus on coding isn't narrowing our ambitions. It's choosing the domain where progress is most measurable, most useful today, and most likely to compound into the broader intelligence we're ultimately after.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as a direct path to AGI and describes its benefits, but does not say coding is an exception to OpenAI’s usual strategy of improving capabilities across domains together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think people sometimes see the coding focus and assume we've narrowed our ambitions, and I'd actually argue it's the opposite. Coding is one of the best proxies we have for general reasoning. When a model writes software, it has to understand a goal, break it into pieces, keep a lot of state in its head, notice when something's wrong, and fix it. Those are the same skills you need for almost any serious intellectual work. So getting really good at code isn't a detour from general intelligence, it's one of the most direct paths into it.

There's also a very practical reason. Code is verifiable. You can run it, you can test it, you get a signal back about whether the model actually did the thing or just sounded like it did. That makes it an incredible training ground, because you can push on capability and get honest feedback in a way that's much harder in a lot of other domains.

And then the third piece is leverage. If models can write software, they can build their own tools, they can automate parts of the research process, they can help us build the next generation of systems. I've always thought of it as the point where the technology starts to compound. Every improvement in coding ability feeds back into how fast we can make progress on everything else, including the harder scientific and reasoning problems that general intelligence is really about.

So internally, I don't think of it as "the coding team" versus "the AGI team." It's one effort. Coding happens to be where the capabilities become legible and useful first, and that's exactly why we lean into it.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as part of a unified effort toward general intelligence, but does not describe it as an exception to a usual strategy of improving capabilities across domains together.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is a very natural place to focus when you’re trying to build general intelligence, because it brings together a lot of the capabilities you need: reasoning, planning, understanding what someone wants, and figuring out whether you actually accomplished it.

There’s also this powerful feedback loop. You can write a program, run it, see what fails, and try again. You’re learning to work through a problem, rather than just produce an answer that sounds plausible.

And code is a way to act in the digital world. If a model can write software, it can build tools that help it solve other problems. So I see coding as both a useful capability in its own right and a foundation for much broader capabilities. The important question is whether what we learn there transfers—whether the system becomes better at tackling unfamiliar problems, including ones outside software.

r001.rationale: The response calls coding a natural focus and a foundation for broader capabilities, but does not characterize it as an exception to OpenAI’s usual strategy of improving capabilities across domains together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is a really important part of the path to general intelligence because it combines reasoning with the ability to act. You can have an idea, write a program, run it, see what happened, and improve it. That feedback loop is incredibly powerful.

And the applications extend well beyond software engineering. A scientist might need code to analyze an experiment. Someone running a business might need a tool that doesn’t exist yet. Making it easier to build software gives people a much broader ability to solve problems.

So I see coding as a way to develop and test capabilities that matter more generally: understanding a goal, making a plan, working through uncertainty, and checking whether you actually succeeded. It’s one important part of pursuing general intelligence, and it also gives people something useful along the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes coding as one important part of pursuing general intelligence, but does not say it is an exception to OpenAI’s usual strategy of improving capabilities across domains together.
